beats.title: Clay Is Fired Into Figurines
beats.description: Hunter-gatherers in central Europe baked moulded clay in a hearth, making the first known ceramic objects.
beats.note: Searched: sources give about 29,000-25,000 years ago; midpoint used.

beats.title: Lime Plaster Is Burned and Made
beats.description: Builders heated limestone and mixed the result with water to make a hard white plaster for floors and walls.
beats.note: Searched: earliest quicklime production put at about 10,400-10,000 BCE; 'Ain Ghazal plaster statues are about 7200 BCE.

beats.title: Copper Is First Smelted
beats.description: People learned to heat copper ore until it ran as liquid metal, the start of making metal rather than just finding it.
beats.note: Approximate; earliest smelting around the Balkans.

beats.title: Gold Is Worked Into Grave Treasure
beats.description: Craftsmen on the Black Sea coast hammered and shaped gold into hundreds of ornaments buried with their dead.

beats.title: Mesopotamians Fire Clay Bricks
beats.description: Builders along the great rivers began baking mud bricks in kilns, making walls that lasted far longer in the damp.
beats.note: Approximate; fired brick appears in the fourth millennium BCE.

beats.title: Bronze Is Alloyed in Sumer
beats.description: Smiths found that mixing tin into copper gave a tougher metal, and an entire age was named after it.

beats.title: Glass Is Made in Mesopotamia
beats.description: Craftsmen melted sand, soda and lime into the first man-made glass, shaped into beads and small vessels.

beats.title: Mesoamericans Cure Natural Rubber
beats.description: Peoples of the Gulf coast mixed latex with plant juice to make bouncing balls and waterproof items.
beats.note: Approximate; earliest evidence of processed latex.

beats.title: The Hittites Master Iron
beats.description: Anatolian smiths began producing iron weapons and tools in quantity, ushering in a harder metal age.
beats.note: Searched: Hittite texts of the 17th-14th centuries BCE mention iron; recent work finds smelted iron in Anatolia from about 2000 BCE, so the date is approximate and contested.

beats.title: Chinese Foundries Pour Cast Iron
beats.description: Furnaces hot enough to melt iron entirely let Chinese founders cast tools and ploughshares in moulds.

beats.title: Indian Smiths Make Wootz Steel
beats.description: Crucible-melted iron with carbon produced a patterned steel that later became legendary for its blades.
beats.note: Searched: first cast put at about 300 BCE; Damascus blades were later made from this steel, so no separate Damascus beat.

beats.title: Romans Perfect Concrete
beats.description: Builders mixed volcanic ash with lime and rubble to make a cement that set even underwater and still stands.
beats.note: Approximate; widely used from the late third to second century BCE.

beats.title: Glassblowing Is Invented
beats.description: Craftsmen on the Syrian coast discovered that molten glass could be inflated on a pipe, making vessels cheap and plentiful.

beats.title: Chinese Potters Fire True Porcelain
beats.description: Kilns reached the heat needed to turn fine white clay into a hard, translucent ceramic.
beats.note: Searched: Britannica says porcelain was first made in the Tang dynasty (from 618); some sources push Han-period precursors earlier.

beats.title: Murano Glassmakers Create Cristallo
beats.description: Venetian glassmakers found a way to make nearly colourless, clear glass fit to rival rock crystal.

beats.title: Lead Crystal Glass Is Patented
beats.description: An English glassmaker added lead oxide to the melt, producing a heavy, brilliant glass that rang when tapped.

beats.title: Europe Finally Makes Porcelain
beats.description: An alchemist in Saxony, ordered to make gold, instead worked out the secret of hard-paste porcelain.
beats.note: Dated to 1708, first successful white porcelain.

beats.title: Darby Smelts Iron With Coke
beats.description: An English ironmaster fuelled his blast furnace with coke instead of charcoal, making iron far cheaper.

beats.title: Huntsman Makes Crucible Steel
beats.description: A Sheffield clockmaker melted steel in clay pots, producing the first uniform, high-quality steel in Europe.

beats.title: Cort Patents Puddled Wrought Iron
beats.description: An English ironmaster stirred molten pig iron to burn off carbon, producing tough bar iron at scale.

beats.title: Portland Cement Is Patented
beats.description: A Leeds bricklayer burned limestone and clay together to make a cement that set like fine stone.

beats.title: Goodyear Vulcanizes Rubber
beats.description: Heating rubber with sulphur stopped it from going sticky in heat and brittle in cold, making it useful.

beats.title: Bessemer Process Makes Cheap Steel
beats.description: Blowing air through molten iron burned out impurities and turned out steel in minutes rather than days.

beats.title: Parkesine, the First Plastic
beats.description: A British chemist showed off a mouldable material made from treated cellulose at a great exhibition.

beats.title: Monier Patents Reinforced Concrete
beats.description: A French gardener embedded iron mesh in concrete to make stronger plant tubs, founding a building revolution.

beats.title: Celluloid Is Patented
beats.description: An American printer sought a billiard-ball substitute and patented a tough, mouldable plastic from cellulose nitrate.

beats.title: Cheap Aluminium Is Smelted
beats.description: Two young chemists independently found that electrolysis of dissolved ore could make the light metal affordable.

beats.title: Bakelite Launches the Plastics Age
beats.description: A Belgian-American chemist created a hard, heat-proof resin made entirely from chemicals, launching the plastics age.

beats.title: Stainless Steel Is Invented
beats.description: A metallurgist adding chromium to steel found it resisted rust and stains, and soon had it made into cutlery.
beats.note: Brearley's 1913 cast is the usual date.

beats.title: Pyrex Glass Goes on Sale
beats.description: A heat-resistant borosilicate glass, first made for railway lanterns, was sold as bakeware for the kitchen.

beats.title: Flexible PVC Is Created
beats.description: An American chemist plasticised a stiff polymer into a soft, versatile vinyl used for pipes, coatings and records.

beats.title: Aerogel Is Made
beats.description: A chemist replaced the liquid in a gel with gas, making a solid that is almost entirely air and a superb insulator.

beats.title: Polyethylene Is Found by Accident
beats.description: Chemists in an English lab found a waxy white solid in a high-pressure experiment, soon the world's commonest plastic.

beats.title: Teflon Is Discovered
beats.description: A DuPont chemist opened a gas cylinder expecting refrigerant and found a slippery white powder that nothing would stick to.

beats.title: PET Plastic Is Patented
beats.description: British chemists patented a clear, strong polyester that later became the standard plastic for drink bottles.

beats.title: Synthetic Diamonds Are Grown
beats.description: A General Electric team squeezed and heated graphite until it crystallised into diamond made by people.

beats.title: Float Glass Revolutionises Windows
beats.description: An English firm floated molten glass on a bath of liquid tin, producing perfectly flat panes cheaply.

beats.title: Kevlar Is Invented
beats.description: A DuPont chemist spun a cloudy polymer solution into an extremely strong material that later stopped bullets.

beats.title: Carbon Nanotubes Are Identified
beats.description: A Japanese physicist spotted tiny hollow tubes of carbon under an electron microscope, stronger than steel.

beats.title: Graphene Is Isolated
beats.description: Two Manchester physicists peeled single-atom-thick sheets of carbon from graphite using sticky tape.
